articles.title: Scrooge screening with live orchestra comes to Heywood Civic
articles.excerpt: The 1951 film starring Alastair Sim will be shown with a live score from the three-piece FB Pocket Orchestra on Saturday 14 November.
articles.content_html:
A screening of the classic film Scrooge with a live three-piece orchestra is coming to Heywood Civic on Saturday 14 November.

The event starts at 8pm and pairs the 1951 film starring Alastair Sim with music performed by the FB Pocket Orchestra. The production is touring in the film’s 75th anniversary year.

The venue lists a running time of 90 minutes. Its Pay What You Can prices are £8.40 at the lower rate, £10.50 standard and £12.60 at the higher rate, all including the booking fee.

Rather than a stage adaptation, this is a showing of the film with live musical accompaniment. It follows Ebenezer Scrooge’s encounters with the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Future in the familiar Charles Dickens story.

The organisers say the music is based on Richard Addinsell’s original score. Heywood Civic’s listing explains that Paul Stevenson reconstructed the score by listening to and transcribing the film soundtrack, creating an arrangement for the ensemble.

The film has a U certificate. For local families and cinema fans, the event offers a chance to hear live musicians accompany a black-and-white Christmas classic at a borough venue.

Heywood Civic is on LCpl Stephen Shaw MC Way, Heywood, OL10 1LW. Tickets and the venue’s pricing information are available at https://heywoodcivic.co.uk/event/scrooge-u-live-to-film/. Check availability and the venue’s accessibility information before booking.

The event was announced in a press release supplied by FB Music and Media, with the date, running time and ticket prices checked against Heywood Civic’s listing on 28 October 2026.

articles.title: Heywood lollipop man forced to leap out of way as drivers ignore crossing
articles.excerpt: A car and a moped have been seized after their drivers failed to stop for a lollipop man in Heywood, forcing him to jump aside for safety.
articles.content_html:
A car and a moped have been seized by Greater Manchester Police after their drivers ignored a lollipop man in Heywood, forcing him to leap out of the way on two separate occasions. The incidents occurred on Bury Old Road on 13 and 14 October, as reported by Rochdale Borough Council.

Barry Jones, the lollipop man involved, was standing in the road when both vehicles failed to stop. The council noted that there have been 137 reported incidents of drivers not stopping for school crossing patrols across the borough in the last five years, highlighting a concerning trend regarding road safety near schools.

Following the incidents, police gathered evidence, including witness statements, which led to the seizure of the silver Skoda car and the moped.

A recent change in law, effective from June, allows police to seize vehicles without issuing a warning first under the Police Reform Act 2002.

Dylan Williams, the cabinet member for highways, expressed gratitude to the police for their prompt action and stated that the council would continue to report such incidents and pursue prosecutions where possible.

This situation underscores the importance of road safety, particularly in school zones, and the need for drivers to adhere to traffic regulations.

articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to enhance the play area at Queen's Park, Heywood, focusing on inclusivity for children with special educational needs.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to MASSEY & HARRIS (ENGINEERING) LIMITED for the Queen's Park SEND and Improvement Project. This initiative aims to create a more inclusive play area at Queen's Park in Heywood, enhancing facilities for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The project will involve several key improvements, including the extension of the existing play area, the installation of a dance arch, the creation of a sensory area surrounding the dance arch, and the addition of a wheelchair swing.

These enhancements are designed to ensure that all children can enjoy the park's facilities, regardless of their physical abilities.

The decision to improve the play area reflects the council's commitment to inclusivity and accessibility in public spaces. By investing in these facilities, Rochdale Council aims to provide a safe and engaging environment for all children in the community, promoting social interaction and play.

The next steps will involve the commencement of construction works, with further updates expected as the project progresses. This development is significant for local families, particularly those with children who have SEND, as it will provide them with improved recreational opportunities in their community.

articles.title: Heywood nursery loses planning bid to keep caravan as outbuilding
articles.excerpt: Little Oaks Nursery in Heywood has been denied permission to retain a caravan used as an outbuilding, following a planning decision by Rochdale Council.
articles.content_html:
Little Oaks Nursery, located on Bamford Road in Heywood, has lost its bid to keep a caravan that replaced a temporary Portakabin in its yard. The nursery applied for retrospective planning permission for the caravan, which has been used as an outbuilding since the Portakabin was removed in 2024 after being granted temporary permission in 2022.

A report from a planning officer indicated that pre-application advice had been sought regarding the placement of a static caravan on the site.

The advice stated that such a structure would not be visually appropriate and would be highly visible from both directions along Bamford Road. Despite this, the caravan was placed on the site without the necessary planning permission, prompting the nursery's application to regulate its presence.

The planning officer's report further noted that the caravan does not meet the high-quality design standards required for a permanent structure.

It was concluded that the caravan does not offer any visual improvement over the temporary Portakabin it replaced, which was only accepted for a limited time due to its unsuitability for permanent retention.

This decision by Rochdale Council highlights ongoing concerns regarding planning regulations and the visual impact of structures within the area. Local residents and businesses may be affected by the enforcement of these regulations, as they aim to maintain the aesthetic integrity of the neighbourhood.

It follows planning permission granted in 2022 for a temporary Portakabin classroom which was removed in 2024. A planning officer’s report said: “Simultaneously, pre-application advice was requested and given for the siting of a static caravan on the site. “The advice given was that such a structure would not be visually appropriate for the site and would be highly visible from both directions along Bamford Road. “Notwithstanding, it appears that a static caravan was nonetheless placed at the site without the benefit of planning permission and this application therefore seeks regulation of such. “The caravan does not provide the high-quality design that officers had previously stated would be required for a permanent structure. “In design terms, the caravan is of no visual improvement over the temporary Portakabin it replaces, which was accepted only for a temporary period on the basis that it was unacceptable for permanent retention. The report added: “The unauthorised screening is insufficient to mitigate this harm, and the development is therefore contrary to policy.” Refusing the application, the council said: “The proposed development, by reason of its siting, massing, design, and temporary utilitarian appearance, would appear as an incongruous, poorly designed feature which would be readily visible from the surrounding street scene by virtue of its prominent location along Bamford Road. “The proposed development would fail to achieve high-quality design and would therefore be harmful to the visual amenities of the area. “The limited public benefits are insufficient to outweigh the harm caused and the proposed development is therefore contrary to Policies DM1 and P3 of the adopted Rochdale Core Strategy, Policy JP-P1 of the Places for Everyone Joint Development Plan, and the National Planning Policy Framework.” The nursery must remove the caravan or appeal the decision. articles.excerpt: GMFRS says firefighters attended for around two hours and 40 minutes after concerns about a building structure. The road's reopening remains unconfirmed.
articles.content_html:
Firefighters attended concerns about a building structure near Bridge Street in Heywood for around two hours and 40 minutes on Saturday 24 October, according to an updated GMFRS statement reported by the Bury Times.

No injuries were reported during these incidents.

The vehicles seized included a moped and a silver Skoda. Police collected evidence, including witness statements, before taking action.

This incident is part of a broader concern, as there have been 137 reported cases of vehicles failing to stop for school crossing patrols in the Rochdale area.

Councillor Williams expressed his dismay at the incidents, stating that such behaviour is unacceptable and poses a significant risk to children. In response to these ongoing safety issues, police have been using body-worn cameras in hotspot areas to deter dangerous driving.

The seizure of these vehicles underscores the need for increased vigilance and compliance with road safety regulations, particularly near schools. Local residents and parents are encouraged to remain alert and report any similar incidents to the authorities.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway steam gala draws more than 2,000 passengers as numbers rise 21.4 per cent
articles.excerpt: Four visiting engines, late trains and a tribute to preservation pioneer Richard Greenwood marked a busy autumn gala on the heritage railway serving Heywood.
articles.content_html:
More than 2,000 passengers visited East Lancashire Railway's Autumn Steam Gala as four visiting locomotives helped deliver a 21.4 per cent increase in passenger numbers on last year's event, according to the railway.

The heritage line, which serves Heywood, held the gala from 16 to 18 October. Three of the four visiting engines were making their first appearances on the ELR, with autumn colours along the Irwell Valley providing the backdrop to a packed weekend of passenger trains, goods workings and late evening journeys.

A first visit from the Bluebell Railway

One of the headline visitors was South Eastern & Chatham Railway Class O1 No. 65, which travelled from the Bluebell Railway for what the ELR described as its furthest ever visit north.

Built at Ashford in 1896 and rebuilt into its present form in 1908, No. 65 appeared in ornate green SECR Wainwright goods livery. It joined resident Lancashire & Yorkshire engines 1300 and 752 in marking significant anniversaries connected with 1896.

Both resident engines received fresh paintwork in lined Lancashire & Yorkshire livery for the gala. No. 1300's finishing touches were completed the day before the event by the railway's resident Heritage Painters team.

Last chance to ride behind visiting pannier tank

Great Western pannier tank No. 7714 arrived from the Severn Valley Railway, courtesy of the SVR Pannier Tank Fund. Built in Stoke-on-Trent by Kerr, Stuart & Co. in 1930, the engine faced south during the gala, giving photographers a different view of the line.

Photographic run pasts with the railway's goods train at Burrs Country Park raised £493 in cash donations. The ELR says passengers have a final opportunity to travel behind No. 7714 on 24 and 25 October before it returns to the West Midlands.

LSWR S15 No. 30506, owned by the Urie Locomotive Society and visiting from the Mid Hants Railway, returned to the ELR for the first time since the 1993 Festival of Steam. It is due to haul scheduled steam services on 31 October and 1 November, as well as taking part in a photographic charter.

The fourth visitor, Hudswell Clarke No. 1208, also made its ELR debut. Usually based at the Embsay & Bolton Abbey Railway and owned by Stephen Middleton, the industrial tank engine worked shuttles to Ramsbottom and paired with No. 65. It carried names from different stages of its working life, including Harold, Illingworth and Mitchell.

Remembering a preservation pioneer

Resident engines City of Wells, Standard 4MT No. 80097 and Lancashire & Yorkshire Pug No. 11243 also featured during the weekend.

Friday included a tribute to preservation pioneer Richard Greenwood, who died earlier this year. Engines 752 and City of Wells, both associated with his preservation work, ran together while his family and friends travelled in the Lancashire & Yorkshire Directors Saloon. The railway said his ashes were scattered into the firebox as the train departed.

Saturday's programme continued after dark, with brake van journeys behind visiting Southern engines, a rare trip into Rawtenstall's bay platform and late passenger workings.

More than 250 volunteer turns

The ELR said more than 250 volunteer turns were needed to deliver the weekend.

General manager Lee Kenny said: “These are results that everyone involved can take pride in. They reflect a great deal of work before the first train runs, throughout the weekend and after the last visitors have gone home.”

He thanked the crews, station teams, stewards, cleaners, catering staff and those responsible for preparing and maintaining the railway, alongside the small team organising the event.

“The gala depends on people across the railway working together, and we are very grateful for the effort and commitment that went into this year's event,” he said.

The railway said the passenger increase helped raise funds for ongoing preservation. Transport for No. 65 was supported by the East Lancashire Railway Preservation Society and a private individual.

What is coming next?

The Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day on 14 November is due to feature engines 752 and 1300 together on the steam service. Pug No. 11243 is also expected to offer short driver experiences around Bury Bolton Street station limits for a small fee. The Directors Saloon is due to offer another opportunity to travel.

The ELR has also announced provisional enthusiast event dates for 2027, when it will mark 40 years since reopening between Bury and Ramsbottom:

6 February: Winter Warmer Diesel Running Day.

19 February: Roch Valley L&Y Pug Railtour Anniversary, with brake van specials planned to mark 60 years since the final Whitworth branch railtours.

20 February: Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day.

12 to 14 March: Spring Steam Gala.

10 April: Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day.

1 to 4 July: Summer Diesel Gala.

23 to 25 July: 40th Anniversary of the ELR Gala.

11 September: L&YR Running Day.

24 to 26 September: Autumn Diesel Gala.

15 to 17 October: Autumn Steam Gala.

6 November: L&YR Running Day.

These dates and locomotive appearances are provisional. Check the railway's latest information before travelling at https://www.eastlancsrailway.org.uk.

Anyone interested in volunteering can find details of departments and recruitment tours at https://www.elrps.co.uk/volunteering.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway secures portable defibrillator for its trains
articles.excerpt: The heritage railway serving Heywood plans to take lifesaving equipment onboard and is seeking support for more mobile units.
articles.content_html:
East Lancashire Railway has secured a portable defibrillator that will eventually travel on its trains, bringing potentially lifesaving equipment closer to passengers, staff and volunteers.

The heritage railway, which serves Heywood, received the Automated External Defibrillator (AED) following fundraising led by ELR Fund Raising Lead Adrian Dewey with support from national charity AEDdonate.

The unit is intended to move with train services rather than remain at a fixed location. It has not yet entered operational service. The railway says it will first establish arrangements for governance, asset management, equipment checks, training and deployment so it can be managed safely as it moves between services.

The new equipment will complement defibrillators already located at stations. ELR hopes to secure further mobile units, with the longer term ambition of extending coverage across all its operating services.

Chairman Mike Kelly said: “Keeping staff, volunteers and our visitors safe is our top priority. I want to thank AEDdonate for their timely donation and all of our kind donors for making this possible.”

He said having equipment available on trains, in addition to station defibrillators, would further strengthen the railway’s health and safety arrangements.

Phillip Warren, ELR Commercial Services Director and AED sponsor, said: “This is about putting lifesaving equipment where our passengers, volunteers and staff actually are.”

He explained that passengers may be travelling somewhere along the line rather than sitting beside a station building, making a portable unit an important additional resource in an onboard emergency.

“Hopefully this equipment will never be needed, but if that day ever comes, we want to have done everything reasonably possible to be prepared,” he said.

The announcement comes during Restart a Heart activity this October. The annual initiative, led by Resuscitation Council UK, promotes awareness of cardiac arrest and CPR education, with Restart a Heart Day held on 16 October.

As a registered charity, ELR relies on fundraising, donations, volunteers and support from businesses and other organisations. It is now inviting individuals to contribute to the next phase of the mobile AED project and businesses to consider sponsoring equipment.

Medical suppliers and other organisations able to donate a unit are also being encouraged to contact the railway.

Warren said: “It is a very tangible way of supporting a charity and potentially helping to save a life.”

Donations towards additional mobile defibrillators can be made through the ELR fundraising campaign: https://www.justgiving.com/campaign/elr-defibrilator-fundraiser

articles.title: Heywood and Middleton North MP visits Redwood School’s sixth form at Phoenix Centre
articles.excerpt: Elsie Blundell, MP for Heywood and Middleton North, visited Redwood School’s sixth form at the Phoenix Centre to engage with students and staff about their educational initiatives.
articles.content_html:
Elsie Blundell, the Member of Parliament for Heywood and Middleton North, visited the Redwood School’s sixth form campus located at the Phoenix Centre in Heywood on October 15. During her visit, she interacted with learners and staff to understand their efforts in supporting young people with special educational needs and disabilities.

Ms Blundell praised the teaching team for their role in helping students build essential skills and confidence for education, adult life, and future employment.

She expressed her pride in having such a facility within her constituency, stating, "I’m so proud to have this facility - and the learners and parents - in my constituency."

The visit included discussions about various lessons, including the importance of recycling. Ms Blundell also enjoyed a meal of soup during her time at the school, which she described as "delicious." She thanked the staff and students for their warm welcome and the valuable lessons shared during her visit.

In her reflections on the day, Ms Blundell commended the young people, parents, teachers, and support staff for their hard work, writing, "Well done again to the young people, parents, teachers and support staff."

This visit highlights the ongoing commitment to enhancing educational opportunities for students with special needs in the Heywood area.

articles.title: Springhill Hospice to host free will information clinic in Heywood
articles.excerpt: Springhill Hospice is offering a free information clinic for those looking to make or update their wills, with expert guidance available.
articles.content_html:
Springhill Hospice will hold a free information clinic aimed at individuals considering making or updating their wills.

The event will take place at the hospice, providing an opportunity for attendees to learn about the importance of having a will and to ask questions regarding the process.

David Copeland, a solicitor from Molesworths Solicitors based in Rochdale, will lead the session. Participants will receive a free will template and refreshments will be provided.

The clinic is designed for anyone, whether they are making their first will or looking to amend an existing one.

Charlotte Mascarenhas, supporter engagement fundraiser at Springhill Hospice, emphasised that the clinic aims to simplify the process of formalising a will, which can often feel daunting for many.

Molesworths Solicitors will waive their usual fees for this service, requesting only a donation to the hospice in return. Springhill Hospice offers care for adults with life-limiting conditions and support for their families across Heywood, Middleton, and Rochdale.

The clinic is open to the public, and there is no obligation to engage further services. Those interested in attending are encouraged to reach out to Springhill Hospice for more details.

The affordability and infrastructure provisions below are recommendations, rather than verified final payments or funded service expansions. In particular, a mixed-purpose contribution must not be reported as wholly dedicated to affordable housing.

No verified site-specific adverse builder finding was established. The public accountability questions are whether the restoration obligations are enforceable, which benefits the eventual payment buys, and when those benefits reach residents.

Russell LDP’s masterplan describes a primary school, local centre, sports pitches, play areas and a 2.2-kilometre link road. Its original hybrid permission dates from March 2020.
articles.content_html:
South Heywood combines an ambition for 1,000 homes with employment development and new community facilities. Russell LDP’s masterplan describes a primary school, local centre, sports pitches, play areas and a 2.2-kilometre link road. Its original hybrid permission dates from March 2020.

The June 2026 council update records continuing Bellway and Anwyl construction and approval of Northstone’s next phase. The link road has opened, according to the project’s announcement. Older forecasts on the masterplan webpage should not be presented as current construction dates.

For residents, the issue is the sequence of delivery. Roads serving new housing and logistics operations do not by themselves establish that classrooms, bus services or medical appointments will be available when families move in. Those questions require the legal obligations, funding and occupation thresholds for each phase.

The published material reviewed does not establish the total number of secured affordable homes or their rents. Individual phases must therefore be assessed separately. Northstone’s homes are already within the 1,000-home masterplan and cannot be added again.

Bellway joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway wins Community Hero Award for its volunteers
articles.excerpt: East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.
articles.content_html:
East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.

The awards celebrate people, groups, charities and businesses that go the extra mile to support others and strengthen their communities. The railway said the recognition reflects the commitment of its volunteers and the role the heritage line continues to play across the communities it serves.

The East Lancashire Railway operates heritage trains through the Irwell Valley, connecting communities including Bury, Summerseat, Ramsbottom, Irwell Vale, Rawtenstall and Heywood.

Diesel Driver and Head of the Signalling Department Linda Henderson said the railway could not exist without its volunteers.

"For almost 40 years, the ELR has operated Heritage trains through the heart of the Irwell Valley. Without volunteers, the ELR and Heritage Railways throughout the UK would not exist."

Henderson said the award recognised more than 800 current volunteers as well as those who had previously given their time to the railway.

Chairman Mike Kelly said he was "extremely proud" to accept the award on behalf of the railway and its volunteers, describing their work as generous and unselfish.

Kelly, who is also a volunteer, said the recognition highlighted the commitment and passion volunteers bring to organisations across local communities. He also thanked Roch Valley Radio for recognising volunteers and the contribution they make to charities and community organisations.

The award was collected by a group of volunteers representing several parts of the railway, including train operations, signalling, the guards department, the dining train team and a station café.

The East Lancashire Railway said the award was a recognition of the hard work and continued dedication of all its volunteers.

articles.title: Heywood councillors vote to end Hopwood Triangle road closure trial
articles.excerpt: Heywood Township councillors have voted unanimously to end the Hopwood Triangle traffic trial after sustained opposition from residents, while the Coronation Avenue HGV parking restriction will remain.
articles.content_html:
Common sense has finally prevailed. At an extraordinary Heywood Township meeting last tonight, councillors voted UNANIMOUSLY to bring the Hopwood Triangle trial on Middleton Road and Magdala Street to an end and remove the road closures. The restriction preventing heavy wagons from parking on Coronation Avenue will remain in place, helping to protect local streets.

For residents, this decision has been a long time coming. The consultation results could hardly have been clearer: 86% of the approximately 700 respondents opposed the scheme. Yet despite that overwhelming response, the trial was approved and went ahead. Residents subsequently raised serious concerns about congestion, access, road safety and the effect on local businesses. People living on Manchester Road also felt they had been left out of the original consultation despite subsequently experiencing the impact of displaced traffic. The timing was another major concern. The trial began during the quieter summer holiday period, with residents warning that the true impact would become much more apparent once schools reopened and normal traffic levels returned. Last night, local people turned out in numbers to make sure their voices were heard. More than 50 residents attended the extraordinary meeting, but the size of the room at the old Police Station quickly became an issue. With residents understandably frustrated about access to a public meeting concerning their own streets, tensions rose and the meeting came close to being suspended. At that point, Reform UK Councillor Stuart Crawford intervened constructively. Recognising that many residents had already heard the Highways presentations and wanted councillors to make a decision, Stuart engaged directly with those in attendance, helped calm the situation and pressed for the meeting to move on to the vote rather than risk the evening ending without a decision. The vote was then taken. Every councillor voted to end the trial. That means the temporary road closures will now be removed, while the restriction on heavy wagons parking on Coronation Avenue will remain. And then there is the cost. The figures presented for the scheme are stark: £110,000 to install the temporary measures. That is £110,000 of public money associated with introducing and then removing a trial which had already been rejected by 86% of consultation respondents. The scheme was voted through back in November by Labour councillors Angela Brown, Paul O’Neil, Peter Hodgkinson, Peter Joinson, Susan Emmott and Liam O’Rourke, despite 86% of consultation respondents opposing it. Last night, the decision went the other way. Whatever political arguments follow, one fact should not be forgotten: local residents spoke up, kept speaking up and ultimately got the result they had been asking for. Reform UK will continue to stand with residents when decisions affecting their communities need to be challenged. A huge thank you to everybody who attended, everybody who responded to the original consultation, and everybody who refused to allow their concerns to be ignored. This was people power in action, and people power won.

The session took place at Unit4 Fitness and began with a group workout before moving into a relaxed social evening. Attendees shared a curry, spent time together and were encouraged to talk openly in an informal setting.

Organisers said it was encouraging to see those attending getting involved, supporting one another and making the most of the opportunity to spend time together.

The event was designed to combine physical activity with peer support and conversation, creating a space where men could connect without the pressure of a formal clinical environment.

WellMental UK thanked everyone who attended and helped make the first Heywood session a success.

The evening marked the beginning of the group's activity in Heywood, with the first session focused on building community, encouraging openness and using fitness as a way to bring people together.

articles.title: Residents furious as waste returns to Heywood alley weeks after major council clean-up
articles.excerpt: Residents say household waste has again been dumped in the alleyway linking Marlborough Street and Canal Street in Heywood, just weeks after council crews carried out a major clearance operation.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Heywood have expressed anger after rubbish was allegedly dumped again in an alleyway just weeks after council crews carried out a major clearance operation.

The alleyway connecting Marlborough Street and Canal Street had previously become heavily cluttered with waste, including discarded food, chairs, refrigerators and freezers. Residents said the accumulation was attracting significant numbers of vermin.

A few weeks ago, two large council vehicles were deployed to clear the alley and remove the accumulated rubbish.

Residents now say household bins have once again been emptied into the alleyway, raising fears that the vermin problem will return.

The repeated dumping is particularly frustrating for families during the summer months. People living nearby say children are being prevented from comfortably using their own backyards because of the rubbish and associated vermin.

One resident described the behaviour as 'extremely selfish, lazy and utterly disgusting' and said photographic evidence and CCTV footage would be submitted to Rochdale Borough Council and Greater Manchester Police.

Residents hope any available footage will help establish who is responsible and allow the relevant authorities to consider enforcement action. No individual has been identified by Rochdale Daily and no assumption should be made about responsibility unless supported by evidence and confirmed by the appropriate authority.

Fly-tipping and repeated waste dumping can create environmental and public-health problems beyond the appearance of an area, particularly where food waste provides a readily available source for rats and other vermin.

For residents who have already seen the alley cleared once, the message is that the community should not have to repeatedly bear the consequences of somebody else's waste.

Anyone with evidence relating to illegal dumping should preserve photographs or CCTV footage and report the matter through the appropriate council or police channels.

articles.title: New grassroots club Heywood Hurricanes FC appeals for raffle prizes to keep football free for every child
articles.excerpt: A brand-new junior football club with one simple goal - making the game accessible to every child regardless of family finances - is asking local businesses to donate raffle prizes.
articles.content_html:
A brand-new grassroots football club in Heywood is appealing to local businesses for raffle prizes as it works to keep the game affordable for every child who wants to play.

Heywood Hurricanes FC has been set up with what it calls one simple goal: to make football accessible for every child. The club says every young player deserves the opportunity to enjoy football, make friends, build confidence and be part of a team - regardless of their family's financial circumstances.

Rather than leaning on sponsorship from the outset, the club is trying to raise funds itself. "As a brand-new club, we're under no illusion that sponsorships are easy to come by," the Hurricanes said. "We know local businesses receive lots of requests, and we completely understand that not everyone is in a position to help financially."

Over the coming weeks the club will hold a raffle to help ease the financial burden on its families and keep costs as low as possible for players. It is asking whether any local businesses would be willing to donate a prize - a voucher, gift hamper, experience, service, or anything else. Every donation, big or small, the club says, will make a genuine difference.

The appeal comes at a time when many families are struggling with the cost of children's sport. Subs, kit, boots and travel add up quickly, and money is increasingly the reason children drop out of the game. By fundraising to keep its own costs down, the Hurricanes hope no child in Heywood is priced off the pitch.

"Your generosity will help us provide opportunities for children to play the game they love without additional financial pressure on their parents, especially at a time when many families are finding things incredibly tough," the club said.

Anyone who would like to support Heywood Hurricanes, or who knows someone who might be able to help, can get in touch by messaging the club's Facebook page.

articles.title: Heywood singer-songwriter releases heartfelt debut single 'Rewind'
articles.excerpt: Twenty-year-old Heywood singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson has achieved a lifelong ambition with the release of her debut single, Rewind, a soulful pop track inspired by heartbreak, hope and moving forward.
articles.content_html:
A young musician from Heywood has realised a lifelong dream with the release of her debut single.

Twenty-year-old singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson released her first original song, Rewind, on 31 July. The soulful pop track draws on her own experience of heartbreak and the realisation that someone she believed was 'the one' ultimately was not the right person after all.

Music has always played a central role in Rhiannon's life, and releasing her own song is something she says she has dreamed about since childhood.

"Having my own song has always been my biggest dream, so finally releasing Rewind is such an emotional and proud moment for me," she said.

Rhiannon worked alongside her friend, songwriter and producer Jack Carroll, who helped write and produce the track in his studio. She cites Sienna Spiro as one of her biggest musical inspirations.

The response to Rewind has already been overwhelming.

"Seeing people say they love my song means everything to me. I hope when people hear it, they remember there is always a light at the end of the tunnel and that things do get better with time."

Looking ahead, Rhiannon hopes to release an EP and continue sharing her music with the world.

"One of my biggest dreams is to hear my music played on the radio. If people enjoy Rewind, I would be so grateful if they could share it and help more people discover my music."

She added: "Thank you to everyone who has supported me so far. I appreciate every listen, every comment and every share — it truly means the world to me."

Rewind is available now on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. Rhiannon can also be followed on Facebook, Instagram at rhiannon_t05 and TikTok at @rhiannonthompsonxx.

articles.title: Veterans invited to weekly breakfast club as Rochdale continues to support Armed Forces community
articles.excerpt: Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being encouraged to attend a free weekly breakfast club in Heywood, offering friendship, support and an opportunity to reconnect with fellow servicemen and women.
articles.content_html:
Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being invited to attend a weekly Armed Forces Breakfast Club held every Thursday morning at The Flying Horse Hotel in Heywood.

Supported by Rochdale Borough Council, the breakfast club has become a welcoming meeting place for former members of the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force. Breakfast is served between 9am and 10am every Thursday, with organisers reporting that thousands of breakfasts have now been served since the initiative began.

While the event offers a free breakfast, its real purpose is bringing veterans together. Leaving military service can often mean leaving behind the camaraderie and close friendships built over years of service. The breakfast club provides an opportunity to reconnect with fellow veterans, share experiences and offer informal peer support in a relaxed environment.

Rochdale has a proud military heritage stretching back generations. The borough has long been associated with the Lancashire Fusiliers and today remains home to a significant Armed Forces community, including serving personnel, reservists, veterans and military families. Many continue serving their communities long after leaving the military through volunteering, public service and local charities.

Research has consistently shown that social connection can play a vital role in improving wellbeing, particularly among veterans who may experience loneliness or find the transition to civilian life challenging. Community initiatives such as breakfast clubs provide an important opportunity to maintain friendships, reduce isolation and ensure no veteran feels forgotten.

The club is open to any military veteran, regardless of how long they served or when they left the Armed Forces. Whether someone completed a full career or served for only a short period, organisers say everyone who has worn the uniform is welcome.

The Armed Forces Breakfast Club takes place every Thursday between 9am and 10am at The Flying Horse Hotel, Heywood.

Rochdale has always been a borough that values those who have served. While remembrance services rightly honour military sacrifice each November, supporting veterans throughout the year is equally important. Initiatives such as the Heywood Breakfast Club demonstrate how something as simple as sharing breakfast can strengthen friendships, improve wellbeing and remind those who have served that their contribution continues to be appreciated by the community.

articles.title: Fresh complaints over persistent landfill odour as Heywood residents report 'sewer' stench and fly infestation
articles.excerpt: Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong foul odour and increasing numbers of flies, prompting renewed questions over the long-running issues surrounding the Pilsworth South landfill site.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong unpleasant smell drifting across parts of the town, with many describing an odour resembling sewage, rotting waste or landfill gas. The latest complaints have reignited concerns over the long-running issues surrounding the nearby Pilsworth South landfill site.

Several residents also reported unusually high numbers of flies, a problem which campaigners have previously associated with the landfill during earlier periods of odour complaints.

Rebecca Hodkinson wrote: "Yep... Unfortunately. And the amount of flies is something else this year."

Billy Casper added: "It stunk rotten like sewers when I was walking up Heywood past Iceland at 5.30 this evening. I don't think it was the landfill though."

Jeanette Noble commented: "I've been smelling it on Darnhill for a few months and the amount of flies is terrible."

Although some residents believe the smell may have originated elsewhere, the recurrence of similar complaints has led many to question whether problems linked to the landfill have returned.

The issue first gained widespread public attention during 2024 when thousands of complaints were submitted to the Environment Agency by residents across Heywood, Middleton, Bury and Rochdale. The smell became one of the borough's most significant environmental concerns, leading to regulatory investigations into landfill gas management and odour control measures at the site.

Under environmental law, landfill sites are permitted to operate only under an Environmental Permit issued by the Environment Agency. Operators are legally required to use Best Available Techniques (BAT) to prevent or minimise pollution, including offensive odours. Persistent smells escaping beyond the site boundary are not automatically unlawful, but they can lead to regulatory enforcement where permit conditions are breached. The Environment Agency has powers to require operational improvements, vary permit conditions, or take enforcement action where appropriate.

The issue has also attracted political attention. West Heywood councillor Angela Brown has repeatedly encouraged residents to report every odour incident directly to the Environment Agency, stressing that detailed reports help investigators establish patterns and build evidence. Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has likewise raised concerns publicly and in Parliament regarding the impact of the landfill on surrounding communities.

Controversy has continued following approval for further landfill operations despite ongoing complaints from nearby residents. Campaigners argue that expansion should not proceed until odour problems have been fully resolved, while regulators maintain that environmental permits require operators to comply with strict controls.

Residents experiencing offensive odours are encouraged to report incidents directly to the Environment Agency, recording the date, time, location, weather conditions and a description of the smell. Multiple reports from different locations can assist investigators in determining whether a wider environmental incident is occurring.

For many residents, the recurring nature of the complaints is becoming increasingly frustrating. While only a full investigation can determine the source of any individual odour event, the persistence of reports over recent years demonstrates that confidence among the local community has yet to be restored.

articles.title: Heywood MP congratulates Bev Craig and calls for stronger investment in the north of the borough
articles.excerpt: Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on becoming Mayor of Greater Manchester, with both Labour politicians expected to work together on transport, regeneration and investment priorities across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on her election as Mayor of Greater Manchester, pledging to work closely with the new mayor to secure investment, improve transport and strengthen opportunities for communities across the constituency.

In a public letter following the mayoral election, Blundell said voters had 'reaffirmed their belief that only Labour can deliver on hopes for a fairer Greater Manchester that works for everyone'. She added that she looked forward to working with the new mayor to grow the economic and cultural future of towns including Bamford, Castleton, Heywood, Middleton, Norden and Spotland.

The MP said her priorities remain focused on creating 'a positive future' for both towns and their residents, supporting jobs, culture and regeneration while responding to the wishes of local communities.

Transport featured heavily in her message. Blundell described the current journey from Heywood into central Manchester by public transport as 'unacceptable', saying many young professionals and families need a quicker and more reliable connection to the city. She reiterated her support for extending Metrolink to Heywood, noting that previous commitments had suggested 'spades in the ground' by 2028, and called for continued confidence in delivering the project.

She also welcomed the success of the Bee Network but stressed that towns outside Manchester city centre must not be left behind. Buses and future tram connections, she argued, both have an important role to play in improving connectivity across the constituency.

Blundell highlighted the opportunities presented by the Mayoral Development Corporations planned for Middleton and Atom Valley, describing them as exciting regeneration projects that could combine investment with skills development for both young and older residents. She said it was essential that local people were first in line to benefit from the jobs and opportunities created by future investment.

For residents across Heywood and the wider Rochdale borough, the relationship between the new Mayor and the local Labour MP could prove significant. With both politicians representing the same party, supporters argue there may be greater scope for joined-up working between Westminster, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority and local councils when bidding for funding, infrastructure projects and devolved investment.

Whether that political alignment ultimately translates into tangible improvements remains to be seen, but transport projects, regeneration schemes and skills investment are all areas where cooperation between regional and national politicians can help unlock funding and accelerate decision-making.

The timing is particularly important for Rochdale Borough Council. The authority has previously warned of significant long-term financial pressures, with forecasts indicating a funding gap that could reach around £16 million by the end of the decade if additional savings or funding are not identified. While the Mayor of Greater Manchester does not directly control council finances, the Combined Authority plays an increasingly important role in distributing regeneration funding, transport investment, housing programmes, brownfield development grants and skills funding across the city-region.

That means a strong working relationship between the Mayor, local MPs and council leaders could improve the borough's chances of securing external investment for projects that might otherwise place further pressure on local budgets. Investment in transport infrastructure, town-centre regeneration and employment initiatives can help stimulate economic growth, attract private investment and broaden the local tax base over time.

However, the partnership alone cannot solve every financial challenge. Local government funding remains largely determined by central government, while council tax income, business rates and rising demand for statutory services continue to place significant pressure on council budgets across England.

Ultimately, constituents will judge the success of the new political partnership not by the warm words exchanged after the election, but by whether it delivers visible improvements. Faster public transport, investment in Heywood and Middleton, better roads, stronger town centres, more employment opportunities and increased funding for local services are among the outcomes residents will hope to see over the coming years.

With both Elsie Blundell and Bev Craig committed to Labour's vision for Greater Manchester, attention now turns from congratulations to delivery. The coming mayoral term will determine whether that political alignment results in lasting benefits for communities across Heywood, Middleton and the wider Rochdale borough.

articles.title: Why are so many taxis in Heywood licensed in Wolverhampton and other areas?
articles.excerpt: Many private hire vehicles working in Heywood display licence plates issued by Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other distant councils. Here is why the practice is legal, why it remains controversial and when an offence may be committed.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Heywood have increasingly been asking the same question: why are so many taxis driving around the town registered in Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other places?

For many people, the sight of private hire vehicles displaying licences issued by councils hundreds of miles away raises concerns about who regulates them, whether they are operating legally and who is responsible if something goes wrong.

The issue has become controversial across England, with local authorities, taxi trade representatives and residents questioning whether the current licensing system gives councils enough control over the vehicles regularly working in their communities.

Why is it controversial?

The debate centres on cross-border licensing.

Since changes introduced under the Deregulation Act 2015, private hire vehicles are no longer expected to work primarily within the area that licensed them. As a result, a driver licensed by Wolverhampton City Council can legally spend most of the working day carrying passengers in Greater Manchester, provided the vehicle and driver comply with the law governing private hire bookings.

Critics argue that the system has weakened local oversight. Drivers may work almost exclusively in Greater Manchester despite being licensed by an authority many miles away, while local councils have less direct control over drivers they did not licence themselves.

Residents may also be unsure which authority they should contact if they wish to make a complaint. Enforcement can become more complicated when several licensing authorities are involved, while different councils may apply different licensing policies and standards.

These concerns have been raised by local authorities across England for several years, with many calling on the Government to reform private hire legislation and give councils greater control over vehicles operating regularly within their boundaries.

Does that mean these vehicles are operating illegally?

No. Although the system is controversial, simply seeing a vehicle licensed in Wolverhampton, Knowsley or another authority driving around Heywood does not mean it is breaking the law.

Private hire licensing works differently from the licensing of traditional taxis.

Unlike a hackney carriage, which can be hailed in the street or wait on an official taxi rank, a private hire vehicle must be pre-booked through a licensed private hire operator before the journey begins.

A Wolverhampton-licensed vehicle seen driving through Heywood could lawfully be travelling to collect a passenger who has already booked, dropping off a customer, waiting for its next booking through an operator or app, or returning from a previous fare.

The licence plate alone does not indicate whether the vehicle is acting lawfully.

When would it become an offence?

The law is much clearer if a private hire vehicle accepts work without a booking.

A private hire driver cannot legally accept passengers who flag the vehicle down in the street, wait on designated taxi ranks or carry passengers without a booking that has first been accepted by a licensed private hire operator.

Those activities are generally reserved for licensed hackney carriage taxis.

If residents witness a private hire vehicle picking up passengers without a booking, licensing officers can investigate whether an offence has been committed.

Who is responsible for enforcement?

One reason the issue generates debate is that responsibility can involve several organisations.

The council that issued the driver's licence retains important regulatory powers and can investigate complaints or suspend and revoke licences where appropriate.

Greater Manchester Police can deal with suspected criminal offences, while local licensing officers may carry out roadside inspections and joint enforcement operations with other authorities.

Many licensing authorities now share intelligence and work together to improve enforcement across council boundaries.

Why Wolverhampton?

Wolverhampton has become one of the country's largest private hire licensing authorities.

Over recent years it has processed applications from drivers across England, meaning many vehicles operating in towns and cities far from the West Midlands legitimately display Wolverhampton licence plates.

The same principle applies to vehicles licensed by authorities such as Knowsley and other councils outside Greater Manchester.

The bigger debate

The growing number of vehicles displaying out-of-area licences has become a national political issue.

Supporters of the current system argue that it provides flexibility for drivers, supports competition and allows passengers to access transport more easily, particularly through app-based booking services.

Critics believe councils should have greater powers over vehicles that spend most of their time working within their communities, regardless of where those vehicles and drivers were originally licensed.

Successive governments have considered reforms to taxi and private hire legislation, but cross-border private hire work remains lawful under the current framework.

What should residents know?

For anyone wondering why so many vehicles in Heywood display Wolverhampton, Knowsley or other out-of-area licence plates, the answer is that the law allows it.

Their presence alone is not evidence of illegal activity.

The important legal question is not where the vehicle is licensed, but whether it is operating as a genuine private hire vehicle, with every journey properly pre-booked through a licensed operator.

Where there is evidence that a private hire vehicle is accepting passengers without bookings or otherwise breaking licensing rules, those concerns can be investigated by the relevant licensing authority and, where appropriate, the police.

articles.title: White Ribbon Football Tournament returns to Rochdale for 2026

articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has confirmed that its annual White Ribbon Football Tournament will return on Tuesday 4 August 2026, bringing together teams from across the council in support of the White Ribbon campaign.

Before kick-off, participating teams will take the White Ribbon pledge, reaffirming their commitment to helping end violence against women and girls.

Residents are encouraged to attend and cheer on the teams throughout the day. While places in the tournament itself are limited, spectators are welcome.

The tournament takes place at Heywood Sports Village on Tuesday 4 August 2026, and spectators are welcome.

The White Ribbon campaign works to engage men and boys in preventing violence against women and girls by promoting positive attitudes, respectful relationships and challenging harmful behaviours.

articles.title: Cloud Gardener Jason Williams to host wellbeing gardening evening in Heywood
articles.excerpt: Television gardening expert Jason Williams will visit Heywood this month for a free community wellbeing event exploring the benefits of container gardening, hosted by Heywood in Bloom as part of the Great Heywood Gathering.
articles.content_html:
Residents are being invited to discover how gardening can support wellbeing when television presenter and horticultural expert Jason Williams visits Heywood later this month for a free community event. Organised by Heywood in Bloom as part of the Great Heywood Gathering programme, the evening will explore how container gardening can improve both physical and mental wellbeing while helping people make the most of even the smallest outdoor spaces.

The event, titled 'Grow Well', will take place on Wednesday, 12 August, from 6.30pm until 9.30pm at Corcoran Close Community Room, Heywood. Organisers say refreshments will be provided free of charge, giving local residents an opportunity to meet others from the community while learning practical gardening techniques from one of the country's best-known horticultural communicators.

Jason Williams, widely known as the 'Cloud Gardener', has built a large following through his work promoting accessible gardening and encouraging people to grow flowers, fruit and vegetables in urban environments. His approach focuses on making gardening achievable for everyone, regardless of the size of their garden or outdoor space, with container gardening becoming increasingly popular among people living in flats, terraces and homes with smaller gardens.

Research continues to demonstrate the benefits gardening can have for health and wellbeing. NHS-backed social prescribing schemes increasingly include community gardening projects as a way of improving mental health, reducing loneliness, encouraging gentle physical activity and strengthening social connections. Studies have also linked time spent in green spaces with reduced stress levels and improved overall wellbeing.

The event forms part of the wider Great Heywood Gathering initiative, supported through the Culture Co-op's Creative People and Places programme. The initiative aims to bring local communities together through arts, culture, wellbeing and environmental activities, encouraging more residents to become involved in projects that improve the town and strengthen neighbourhood connections.

Heywood in Bloom has played an important role in enhancing public spaces across the town through volunteer-led planting schemes, community gardening projects and environmental improvements. Working alongside residents, schools and community organisations, the group has helped transform flower beds, public spaces and neglected areas while promoting biodiversity and civic pride.

The event has been supported by Rochdale Borough Council, Your Trust, Arts Council England, The National Lottery Community Fund and Pride in Place, reflecting the collaborative approach taken to delivering community activities across the borough.

Organisers hope the evening will inspire more people to discover the benefits of gardening, whether by growing flowers on a balcony, vegetables in containers or creating wildlife-friendly spaces at home. They also hope the event will encourage new volunteers to become involved with Heywood in Bloom and future environmental projects across the town.

Anyone interested in attending is encouraged to arrive in time for the 6.30pm start at Corcoran Close Community Room, OL10 4XD. With expert advice, free refreshments and a focus on community wellbeing, organisers hope the evening will leave attendees with practical ideas, new friendships and the confidence to start growing at home.
